original_question: Is it true that oral erythroplakia carries a higher risk of progressing to the most common type of head and neck cancer compared to oral leukoplakia?

final_qi.question: Does oral erythroplakia carry a higher risk of progressing to the most common type of head and neck cancer?
final_qi.long_answer: The most prevalent malignancy arising in the head-and-neck region is squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Oral erythroplakia is defined as a persistent, homogeneously red, velvety mucosal lesion that cannot be clinically or histopathologically characterized as another condition. Multiple large biopsy series have shown that 80–90 % of erythroplakic lesions already contain severe epithelial dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, or frankly invasive squamous cell carcinoma at the time of diagnosis, and prospective studies report malignant transformation rates far higher than those for other oral potentially malignant disorders such as leukoplakia (often estimated at ≥15-20 % within a few years). Because of this very high prevalence of high-grade dysplasia and its frequent evolution into invasive squamous cell carcinoma, oral erythroplakia is regarded as one of the lesions with the greatest propensity to progress to the common head-and-neck cancer type. Thus, the statement that oral erythroplakia carries a higher risk of progressing to the most common form of head and neck cancer (squamous cell carcinoma) is supported by established medical evidence.

final_qi.question: Does oral leukoplakia carry a risk of progressing to the most common type of head and neck cancer?
final_qi.long_answer: Oral leukoplakia is classified as an oral potentially malignant (premalignant) disorder. Numerous longitudinal studies show that a proportion of these lesions (roughly 1–20 % depending on size, dysplasia grade, anatomic site, tobacco/alcohol use, etc.) undergo malignant transformation. The cancer that develops almost invariably is oral squamous cell carcinoma—the same histologic type that constitutes the vast majority (>90 %) of head and neck cancers overall. Therefore, oral leukoplakia does carry a proven risk of progressing to the most common form of head and neck cancer.
